newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals lack robust consumer interest.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals lack robust consumer interest.

text.p: Trading in the industrial minor metals held few surprises over the past week and prices tended to remain at little changed amid the lack of strong consumer participation.
Volumes remained thin, apart from gallium, which for a metal recently languishing in the doldrums found fairly brisk enquiry from Japanese and US based end-users.
Demand for communication satellites and hi-tech blue laser production may spark a further rise in gallium prices.
It is used in solar panels, an energy source of many satellites, traders said.
Traders said the market looks poised to advance further against the backdrop of low stocks.
Japanese enquiry helped to lift gallium, against the backdrop of low stocks.
Antimony held steady and took a breather from recent sharp gains.
Traders said Chinese offers were few and far between, but consumer demand remained at a low ebb.
"The recent panic to cover on the upside has slowed, though I am still unsure of antimony's next direction" one trader said.
Traders noted China's exports of unwrought antimony rose to 31,192 tonnes in 1996, up by 22.5 percent compared with a year ago.
Antimony exports were 3,345 tonnes in December.
Several traders suggested the recent rally from a mid-December low of $2,050/$2,150 a tonne was set to continue near-term and pegged an upside target at around $2,500 or higher.

They argued Chinese producers were holding back for higher prices and that stocks were running at low levels -- a condition that was unlikely to satisfy first and second quarter 1997 consumer requirements.
Others said the market was fast becoming overbought and was due for a downside correction following the steady gains during the early part of this year.
Germanium which was expected to drift back after a recent price surge continued to find keen buying, though several traders were unsure how long the high numbers could be maintained.
Both high and low nitre content chrome were underpinned by demand from the aerospace industry.
Traders said most of the minor metals linked to the aerospace industry were currently experiencing upside interest. Traders said chrome was aided by a lack of Chinese material.
Recently two sources said Russian producers were late in delivering material to a market already gripped by supply tightness.
Molybdenum was also underpinned by the aircraft sector and to a lesser extent from the hi-tech electronics industry.
Magnesium eased under Ukrainian and Chinese offers. Bismuth drifted in light trading, while indium on Japanese and US demand was looking to head higher on the back of hi-tech industry demand.
Titanium sponge held firm on demand from the aerospace industry.
Russian cobalt drifted, as did high grade material, though fundamentally they both looked strong.
Manganese eased despite a fall in China's exports of unwrought manganese to 45,652 tonnes in 1996, down by 9.1 percent compared with a year ago, customs figures showed on Thursday.
